# Security Policy

This document is the **vulnerability disclosure policy** for this repository — how to report a
security problem in the starter itself.

It is not the API security guide. For how authentication, RBAC, password handling, token lifecycle,
rate limiting, validation, and security headers actually work in this template, read
[`docs/SECURITY.md`](../docs/SECURITY.md).

## Supported versions

This is a starter template rather than a versioned library. Security fixes land on `main`, and
projects built from the template are expected to pull them forward themselves. Only the current
`main` branch is supported.

## Reporting a vulnerability

**Do not open a public issue for a security vulnerability.**

Report it privately through GitHub Security Advisories:

<https://github.com/aolus-software/clean-hono/security/advisories/new>

That creates a private thread visible only to the maintainers. If you cannot use GitHub Advisories,
open a regular issue that says only "security report, please provide a private contact" with no
technical detail, and a maintainer will follow up.

Please include, as far as you can determine it:

- the affected component (middleware, guard, module route, repository, config) and `file:line` if
  you have it,
- the conditions required to reach it — authenticated or not, which role or permission, which data,
- a proof-of-concept request or sequence,
- the impact you believe it has.

You should get an acknowledgement within a few days. Please give the maintainers a reasonable window
to ship a fix before disclosing publicly.

## Scope

In scope — anything that ships in this repository:

- authentication and token handling: `AuthMiddleware`
  (`src/libs/hono/middlewares/security/auth.middleware.ts`), the JWT helper in
  `src/libs/utils/hono/jwt.ts` (access and refresh tokens, `type` claim), and the
  `src/modules/auth/` flows (login, refresh, register, email verification, password reset),
- the cache-aside user lookup in `AuthMiddleware` — in particular stale reads of
  `UserInformationCacheKey` after a role, permission, or status change,
- the RBAC layer: the permission and role guards in `@guards`, the `superuser` short-circuit, and any
  route whose `middleware` gating can be bypassed,
- soft delete: reads that forget `deleted_at IS NULL` and let deleted users be read back
  (`.claude/rules/repositories.md`),
- secret handling: bcrypt password hashing (`Hash` in `@utils`), `APP_KEY`, `JWT_SECRET`,
  `JWT_REFRESH_SECRET`, the crypto-js `EncryptionToolkit`, and anything leaking secrets into logs,
  responses, or OpenAPI examples,
- the security middlewares under `src/libs/hono/middlewares/security/`: CORS, security headers, the
  100-requests-per-60-seconds rate limiter, and the body limit,
- Zod validation gaps that let unvalidated input reach a service or a query,
- query-shape problems in `src/libs/database/postgres/repositories/` — including unwhitelisted sort
  keys or filter keys reaching a Drizzle `orderBy` / `where`,
- BullMQ job payloads that carry secrets, or workers that can be driven by attacker-controlled data
  (`src/bull/`),
- the OpenAPI surface at `/docs` exposing schemas or examples it should not,
- dependency vulnerabilities that are reachable through code in this repo.

Out of scope:

- vulnerabilities in a project _built_ from this template that come from that project's own code,
- anything requiring a misconfiguration the docs tell you not to ship — for example leaving
  `ALLOWED_HOST` empty, keeping the example `APP_KEY` / `JWT_SECRET` / `JWT_REFRESH_SECRET`, or
  setting `ENABLE_API_DOCS=true` in production,
- missing hardening that is documented as the deployer's responsibility (TLS termination, database
  and Redis network access, secret storage, ClickHouse exposure),
- reports generated by an automated scanner with no demonstrated exploit path.

## Known hardening notes

These are documented rather than treated as vulnerabilities. Review them before deploying:

- `.env` holds every secret and is never committed. **`JWT_SECRET` and `JWT_REFRESH_SECRET` have no
  envalid default** — the process refuses to boot without them. Use two different values. Rotate
  `APP_KEY` away from its `.env.example` placeholder too; envalid _does_ supply a default for that
  one, so the app starts with an insecure value.
- Access tokens live 1 day, refresh tokens 7 days. The current refresh-token id is
  stored in Redis per user and rotated on every refresh, so a refresh token works once; password
  changes and resets, user deletion, and deactivation revoke it.
- `ALLOWED_HOST` feeds the CORS origin list. Set it to your real front-end origins as a
  comma-separated list; an empty value means every origin.
- The Scalar/OpenAPI reference at `/docs` (and `/docs/openapi.json`) is served only when
  `ENABLE_API_DOCS=true`. It defaults to `false`; `.env.example` turns it on for local development.
- The rate limiter is global at 100 requests per 60 seconds per client IP, in memory. In cluster
  mode each worker keeps its own counter, so the effective limit is multiplied by the worker count.
  Put a shared limiter (reverse proxy or Redis store) in front before exposing the API.
- The body limit caps request bodies at 100KB. Raise it deliberately, per route, rather than
  globally.
- Redis (`REDIS_PASSWORD`) backs both the cache and BullMQ. Anything that can write to that Redis can
  forge cached user information and enqueue jobs.
- The seeder in `src/libs/database/seed/` creates `superuser@example.com` and `admin@example.com`,
  both with the password `S3crEtP4ssw0rd!`, already email-verified. Change or remove them before any
  deployment that is reachable from the internet.
- The Husky `pre-commit` hook runs `drizzle-kit migrate` against the `DATABASE_URL` in your `.env`. Do
  not let that point at production. See `.github/CONTRIBUTING.md`.
